title: Cuellar Lays Out Plans as Incoming Homeland Security Spending Chair
excerpt: U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar says accountability for border spending will be his top priority when he becomes chairman of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security in January, and he plans to scrutinize about $260 billion in Homeland Security funding approved outside the regular budget process.
content:
U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar says accountability for border spending will be his top priority when he becomes chairman of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security in January, when Democrats take control of the House, according to the Laredo Morning Times.

Cuellar said at a recent media briefing that the post will give border lawmakers a larger voice in decisions on immigration enforcement, border infrastructure and the Department of Homeland Security.

He plans to scrutinize roughly $260 billion in Homeland Security-related funding that was approved outside the regular appropriations process. He told the Rio Grande Guardian that, by his count, $113 billion went to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, $46.5 billion to border barriers and buoys, and $27 billion to the Homeland Security secretary’s office. In an interview published Nov. 23, Cuellar said he wants guardrails on Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a detailed accounting of the money, according to the Rio Grande Guardian.

Cuellar, 71, won a 12th term Nov. 3, beating Republican Tano Tijerina. “For the first time, we’re going to have a chairman from the border for Homeland Security,” he said on election night. His new term begins Jan. 3, 2027.

Cuellar also voiced support for a bipartisan permitting reform bill that would speed approvals for energy and electric-grid projects, and said he would like to see it pass before January.

With a Dec. 11 funding deadline ahead and 12 appropriations bills still pending, Cuellar said he expects Congress to pass several bills and use a short-term continuing resolution to carry the government into February. He said he does not expect a government shutdown.

He also addressed sections of the Rio Grande buoy barrier in Laredo that reportedly broke loose again, and a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop ahead of Thanksgiving that disrupted air travel.
